28774:
Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, from a priestly family at Anathoth, was called as a young man in 627 BC and prophesied for some forty years through the last kings of Judah, the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC, and its aftermath. Forbidden to marry, opposed by his own townsmen, beaten, imprisoned, and nearly killed more than once, he insisted that Judah's only path was repentance and then submission to Babylon, a message that made him look like a traitor.

The book reveals his inner life more than any other prophet's. In passages often called his 'confessions' he argues with God, curses the day of his birth, and yet finds the word like fire shut up in his bones that he cannot hold in. He performs striking sign-acts: a ruined linen belt, a smashed flask, a wooden yoke, a field purchased while the city is falling. With his scribe Baruch he produced written scrolls of his oracles, one of which King Jehoiakim burned.

Alongside judgment he announced hope: a seventy-year limit to exile, return to the land, and a new covenant written on the heart. That promise became foundational for the New Testament's understanding of Jesus' death and the church (Luke 22:20; Heb 8:8-12). His last known words were spoken in Egypt, where he had been taken against his will.

28862:
Ezekiel son of Buzi was a priest deported to Babylonia with King Jehoiachin in 597 BC. Five years later, beside the Chebar canal, he saw the glory of God enthroned above living creatures and wheels, and was commissioned to speak to a rebellious people whether they listened or not. For more than twenty years he ministered among the exiles at Tel-abib, where the elders came to sit in his house.

His ministry falls into two halves divided by the fall of Jerusalem. Before 586 BC he insisted, against the exiles' hopes, that the city and temple would be destroyed because of idolatry; he acted this out through startling sign-acts and long allegories of Jerusalem as an unfaithful wife, and he saw the glory of God depart from the temple. After the news of the city's fall reached him, his message turned to restoration: a new heart and spirit, a shepherd-king from David's line, dry bones raised, and a renewed temple from which a life-giving river flows.

Ezekiel addresses the individual's responsibility before God (Ezek 18), the honour of God's name among the nations, and the reality of God's presence outside the land. His imagery is reused extensively in the book of Revelation.

He was made a watchman (Ezek 3:17; Ezek 33:7), was periodically unable to speak except to deliver God's word (Ezek 3:26-27; Ezek 24:27; Ezek 33:22), lived in a house where elders consulted him (Ezek 8:1; Ezek 14:1; Ezek 20:1), and was widowed (Ezek 24:18).
